members.r: Digital Services Act and Platform Regulation Research
AI Act, Soft Law and Standards Research

governance_justification: The binding, horizontal and risk-tiered AI Act anchors the regime and the coded guidelines and codes operationalise it, while the GDPR, Law Enforcement Directive, DSA and Platform Work Directive add sectoral and data-protection duties, which makes Hybrid a credible but weaker alternative.
institutional_map: Enforcement is split. The Commission's AI Office supervises general-purpose AI models and, since 2 August 2026 under Article 75(1) as replaced by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, is exclusively competent, with its own fining powers, for providers of AI systems built on their own GPAI models (save listed exceptions such as Annex I products, critical infrastructure, law-enforcement and justice uses) and of AI in very large online platforms and search engines; market surveillance authorities designated by each Member State enforce the AI Act for all other systems, the EDPS does so for EU institutions, notified bodies carry out third-party conformity assessment, and the European AI Board coordinates. National data protection authorities, with the EDPB, enforce GDPR Articles 22 and 35, the Law Enforcement Directive and the data-protection parts of the Platform Work Directive, whose other provisions fall to authorities each Member State designates. Digital Services Coordinators and the Commission enforce the DSA. The main overlaps are the Commission's double role over very large platforms under both the DSA and the AI Act, and the shared ground of data protection and market surveillance authorities on biometrics and automated decisions.
conv: Like China's labelling measures and India's 2026 rules on synthetically generated information, the EU now requires machine-readable marking of AI-generated content and disclosure of deep fakes (AI Act Art 50, applicable from 2 Aug 2026, and from 2 Dec 2026 for marking by generative systems already on the market).

As in China's Personal Information Protection Law (Art 24), the individual's main rights against automated decisions sit in general data-protection law (GDPR Art 22, Law Enforcement Directive Art 11) rather than in the AI statute, which relies mainly on duties enforced by regulators.
gaps: Rights of affected people are thin and fragmented: the AI Act offers only a complaint to a market surveillance authority and an explanation for Annex III decisions, so contesting a decision supported by AI depends on the GDPR, DSA, Platform Work Directive or national law. The AI Liability Directive proposal was withdrawn in 2025, so fault-based claims for AI harm rest on national law, with the revised Product Liability Directive covering defective software only for products placed on the market after 9 Dec 2026.

The framework is not yet operative where risk is highest: Annex III high-risk duties apply only from 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I duties from 2 Aug 2028, the first harmonised standard (EN 18286:2026, on quality management) was cited only in October 2026, and the GDPR reform on AI training and automated decisions is still being negotiated.
assume: Ten instruments are coded. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) is folded into the AI Act row because its operative changes are to that Act; its aviation and machinery amendments are consequential. Excluded: the Commission's AI-system definition guidelines (C(2025) 5053), which interpret a definition and impose no duties; the DSA guidelines on protection of minors, which are general child-safety guidance; and, because no accepted team coded them, the Product Liability Directive, the Council of Europe Framework Convention, the GPAI scope guidelines, the Article 50 code of practice and harmonised standards. National transposition is not coded. Judgement calls: directives are coded Statute; codes of practice Regulator guidance; importers and distributors are folded into Developer and Deployer; public authorities are coded State; the DSA's size-based tiers are not treated as risk classification. Official English texts were used, so there is no translation risk. Disagreement: NUA coded the Platform Work Directive as defining AI, LexBharata did not; the editors followed the text, which defines only automated monitoring and decision-making systems, and coded No. All three teams chose Comprehensive statute, two noting Hybrid as an alternative; the editors kept Comprehensive statute. Status verified as of 19-11-2026.

instruments.name: General Data Protection Regulation, Article 22 (automated individual decision-making, including profiling)
instruments.systems: Decisions based solely on automated processing, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects; technology-neutral, so it reaches AI scoring and decision tools
instruments.trigger: A controller takes a solely automated decision that produces legal or similarly significant effects for a person; applicable since 25 May 2018
instruments.duty_note: Such decisions are barred unless necessary for a contract, authorised by law or based on explicit consent; where allowed, the controller must give meaningful information about the logic involved and safeguards including human intervention
instruments.enf: National data protection supervisory authorities, with consistency ensured through the European Data Protection Board
instruments.remedy: Administrative fines up to EUR 20m or 4% of worldwide annual turnover (Art 83(5)); complaints, judicial remedies and compensation (Arts 77-82)
instruments.gap: The 'solely automated' threshold and the contract, law and consent exceptions leave much decision-making supported by AI outside the rule, so nominal human involvement can defeat it. The Court of Justice has narrowed this gap by treating a decisive credit score as an automated decision (SCHUFA, C-634/21) and by requiring the logic of a decision to be explained (Dun & Bradstreet Austria, C-203/22).
instruments.citation: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1, art 22 (with arts 13(2)(f), 14(2)(g), 15(1)(h))

instruments.name: General Data Protection Regulation, Article 35 (data protection impact assessment)
instruments.systems: Personal-data processing likely to pose a high risk, expressly including new technologies and systematic, extensive automated evaluation (profiling) on which significant decisions are based
instruments.trigger: Before processing that is likely to result in a high risk to individuals begins (Art 35(1), (3)); national supervisory-authority lists specify when an assessment is required
instruments.duty_note: The controller must assess the necessity, proportionality and risks of the processing, set out mitigating measures, and consult the supervisory authority first if high risk remains (Art 36)
instruments.remedy: Administrative fines up to EUR 10m or 2% of worldwide annual turnover (Art 83(4)); corrective orders under Art 58
instruments.gap: The assessment is internal: it need not be published or shared with the people affected. Because the trigger is high-risk processing of personal data rather than AI use, AI systems that run on anonymised or non-personal data escape it.
instruments.citation: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1, arts 35-36

instruments.name: Law Enforcement Directive, Article 11 (automated individual decision-making)
instruments.systems: Solely automated decisions, including profiling, taken by competent authorities for criminal-law purposes; technology-neutral, so it covers AI-based risk assessment
instruments.trigger: A competent authority takes a solely automated decision with an adverse legal effect or significant effect on a person in preventing, investigating, detecting or prosecuting crime or executing penalties
instruments.duty_note: Member States must prohibit such decisions unless a law authorises them with safeguards including at least human intervention, and must prohibit profiling that discriminates on the basis of special categories of data
instruments.enf: National supervisory authorities designated under the Directive (Art 41)
instruments.remedy: Penalties set by Member States (Art 57) and a right to compensation for damage (Art 56)
instruments.gap: Beyond human intervention it leaves safeguards to national law, with no express right to an explanation or to contest, so protection against AI-driven policing varies by country and overlaps unclearly with the AI Act's law-enforcement high-risk category.
instruments.citation: Directive (EU) 2016/680 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data by competent authorities for the purposes of the prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or the execution of criminal penalties, and on the free movement of such data, OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 89, art 11

instruments.name: Digital Services Act
instruments.systems: Recommender, content-moderation and advertising systems of intermediary services, with extra duties for very large online platforms and search engines (45 million or more monthly EU users); not an AI-specific law
instruments.trigger: Offering intermediary services to recipients in the Union; fully applicable since 17 Feb 2024, with very-large-platform duties applying four months after designation
instruments.duties: Transparency; Risk management; Audit; Human oversight
instruments.duty_note: Platforms disclose the main parameters of recommender systems (Art 27), give reasons for moderation decisions and decide complaints not solely by automated means; very large services assess and mitigate systemic risks, undergo independent audits and offer a feed not based on profiling (Arts 34-35, 37-38)
instruments.enf: National Digital Services Coordinators; the European Commission for very large online platforms and search engines
instruments.remedy: Fines up to 6% of worldwide annual turnover and periodic penalty payments up to 5% of average daily turnover; compensation claims by recipients (Art 54)
instruments.gap: It reaches AI only through recommender and moderation functions and requires disclosure of 'main parameters' rather than an auditable account of how a model behaves. For AI built into very large platforms, Commission supervision under the DSA now overlaps with the AI Office's exclusive AI Act competence added in 2026 (Art 75(1)(b) AI Act).
instruments.citation: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single Market For Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act), OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, p. 1, arts 17, 20, 27, 34-35, 37-38

instruments.name: Artificial Intelligence Act
instruments.systems: Horizontal and risk-tiered: prohibited practices (Art 5, extended in 2026 to AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material), high-risk systems (Art 6, Annexes I and III), Art 50 transparency systems and general-purpose AI models (Chapter V)
instruments.trigger: Placing on the market, putting into service or use of AI in the Union; phased: bans and AI literacy from 2 Feb 2025, GPAI duties from 2 Aug 2025, Art 50 from 2 Aug 2026, new bans from 2 Dec 2026, Annex III high-risk duties from 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I from 2 Aug 2028 (dates as amended by Reg (EU) 2026/1744)
instruments.duties: Prohibition; Risk management; Data governance; Human oversight; Transparency; Labelling; Impact assessment; Registration or filing
instruments.duty_note: Bans listed practices; high-risk providers must run risk management and data governance, design for human oversight, pass conformity assessment and register; some deployers must assess fundamental-rights impact; Art 50 disclosure and marking; documentation and systemic-risk duties for GPAI model providers
instruments.tiers: Prohibited; High-risk; Transparency (limited) risk; Minimal; plus GPAI models and GPAI models with systemic risk
instruments.enf: National market surveillance authorities; the Commission's AI Office for GPAI models and, since 2 Aug 2026, exclusively for providers of AI systems built on their own GPAI models (save listed exceptions such as Annex I products, critical infrastructure, law-enforcement and justice uses) and of AI in very large online platforms and search engines (Art 75(1)); the EDPS for EU institutions; the European AI Board coordinates
instruments.remedy: Fines up to EUR 35m or 7% of worldwide turnover for prohibited practices, EUR 15m or 3% for most other duties and EUR 7.5m or 1% for misleading information (Art 99), with lower caps for SMEs and, except for prohibited practices, small mid-caps; AI Office fines and periodic penalties for operators in its competence (Art 75c); Commission fines on GPAI providers (Art 101); withdrawal or recall
instruments.gap: Affected persons get only a right to complain to a market surveillance authority (Art 85) and to an explanation of decisions based on Annex III high-risk outputs (Art 86), with no AI Act right to contest a decision or obtain compensation. The core high-risk regime is also deferred, to 2 Dec 2027 for Annex III and 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I systems.
instruments.citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act), OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024; as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 (Digital Omnibus on AI), OJ L, 2026/1744, 24.7.2026

instruments.name: Platform Work Directive
instruments.systems: Automated monitoring and decision-making systems that digital labour platforms use to manage people performing platform work (algorithmic management); technology-neutral
instruments.trigger: A digital labour platform uses automated monitoring or decision-making systems on people performing platform work; in force since 1 Dec 2024, with national transposition due by 2 Dec 2026 (Art 29)
instruments.duties: Prohibition; Data governance; Impact assessment; Transparency; Human oversight
instruments.duty_note: Bars processing such as emotional-state, private-conversation and sensitive-trait inference (Art 7); requires data protection impact assessments (Art 8), disclosure of the systems (Art 9), human oversight with power to override (Art 10) and explanation and review of significant decisions (Art 11)
instruments.enf: Data protection authorities for the data-protection aspects of Arts 7-11, alongside labour and other competent authorities designated by each Member State (Art 24); no EU-level enforcer
instruments.remedy: Penalties set by Member States, with the GDPR Art 83(5) fine ceiling applying to breaches of Arts 7-11; dispute resolution and redress including compensation (Art 18)
instruments.gap: It protects only people working through digital labour platforms, leaving algorithmic management in conventional workplaces outside its reach, and its practical content depends on national transposition due by 2 Dec 2026.
instruments.citation: Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on improving working conditions in platform work, OJ L, 2024/2831, 11.11.2024

instruments.name: Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act)
instruments.systems: AI systems used for the practices banned by Art 5 AI Act as first enacted, e.g. harmful manipulation, social scoring, untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion recognition at work or school, and real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement
instruments.trigger: Placing on the market, putting into service or use of an AI system for an Art 5 practice; the bans have applied since 2 Feb 2025 and the fines since 2 Aug 2025
instruments.duty_note: Explains the scope of each ban and its exceptions with practical examples; creates no obligations of its own
instruments.enf: National market surveillance authorities enforce Art 5, and the AI Office does so for systems within its exclusive competence (Art 75(1), as amended in 2026); the Commission issues the guidance
instruments.remedy: None in the guidelines; breaches of Art 5 carry fines up to EUR 35m or 7% of worldwide turnover (Art 99(3) AI Act)
instruments.gap: Being non-binding, they cannot settle the contested edges of the bans (manipulation, emotion recognition, biometric categorisation), which only the Court of Justice can do. They also do not address the bans on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material added in 2026, which apply from 2 Dec 2026.
instruments.citation: European Commission, Communication C(2025) 5052 final of 29 July 2025, Commission Guidelines on prohibited artificial intelligence practices established by Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) (content approved on 4 February 2025, C(2025) 884 final)

instruments.name: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
instruments.systems: General-purpose AI models, with a Safety and Security chapter that applies only to models with systemic risk
instruments.trigger: Voluntary signature by GPAI model providers; the underlying AI Act duties apply from 2 Aug 2025 (from 2 Aug 2027 for models already on the market), with Commission fining powers from 2 Aug 2026
instruments.duty_note: Signatories commit to model documentation, a policy for complying with EU copyright law and, for systemic-risk models, assessment and mitigation of safety and security risks
instruments.tiers: GPAI models; GPAI models with systemic risk
instruments.enf: The AI Office of the European Commission
instruments.remedy: None for breach of the Code as such; GPAI providers face Commission fines up to EUR 15m or 3% of worldwide turnover under Art 101 AI Act
instruments.gap: Adherence is voluntary and confers no presumption of conformity, only a recognised way to demonstrate compliance, so the practical content of the GPAI duties rests on AI Office enforcement discretion. Downstream deployers and affected people are protected only indirectly.
instruments.citation: European Commission (AI Office), General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, 10 July 2025; assessed as adequate by Commission Opinion C(2025) 5361 final of 1 August 2025

instruments.name: Commission Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of the AI Act
instruments.systems: AI systems that interact directly with people, generate or manipulate synthetic content, perform emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, or produce deep fakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest
instruments.trigger: Art 50 duties apply from 2 Aug 2026; providers of generative systems placed on the market before then have until 2 Dec 2026 to meet the Art 50(2) marking duty (Art 111(4), inserted by Reg (EU) 2026/1744)
instruments.duty_note: Explains when people must be told they are dealing with an AI system, how synthetic content must be marked in machine-readable, detectable form, and when deep fakes and AI-generated public-interest text must be disclosed
instruments.enf: National market surveillance authorities; the AI Office for provider duties of systems in its Art 75(1) competence (deployer duties only where it is also the deployer); the EDPS for EU institutions; the Commission issues the guidance
instruments.remedy: None in the guidelines; breaches of Art 50 carry fines up to EUR 15m or 3% of worldwide turnover (Art 99(4) AI Act)
instruments.gap: Being non-binding, they cannot fix a technical benchmark for marking and detection, which is left to the voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content (June 2026) and to future standards. Providers and deployers that do not sign the code must show compliance by other adequate means, assessed case by case by the competent authority.
instruments.citation: European Commission, Communication C(2026) 7702 final of 5 November 2026, Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the 'AI Act'), OJ C, C/2026/6005, 12.11.2026 (content approved on 20 July 2026, C(2026) 5054 final)

instruments.name: Digital Omnibus proposal (amendments to the GDPR and other data rules)
instruments.systems: Personal-data processing for developing and operating AI systems and models, and solely automated decisions under GDPR Art 22; refers to the AI Act definition of an AI system
instruments.trigger: Would apply only once adopted; Council negotiating mandate agreed on 21 Oct 2026, Parliament still at committee stage on 19 Nov 2026, so trilogues have not begun
instruments.duty_note: Would recognise legitimate interest as a basis for processing personal data to develop and operate AI, with safeguards including an unconditional right to object (new Art 88c), and recast the Art 22 conditions for solely automated decisions
instruments.enf: National data protection authorities and the European Data Protection Board (GDPR machinery unchanged)
instruments.remedy: GDPR sanctions machinery (Art 83 fines up to EUR 20m or 4% of turnover) would apply
instruments.gap: As proposed it would ease AI training on personal data and recast Art 22 from a right into a list of permitted cases; the Council mandate restores the right-based Art 22 wording but refers to the ordinary Art 21 objection right instead of an unconditional one. With no Parliament position, the rules for AI-related processing remain unsettled.
instruments.citation: European Commission, Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council amending Regulations (EU) 2016/679, (EU) 2018/1724, (EU) 2018/1725, (EU) 2023/2854 and Directives 2002/58/EC, (EU) 2022/2555 and (EU) 2022/2557 as regards the simplification of the digital legislative framework, and repealing Regulations (EU) 2018/1807, (EU) 2019/1150, (EU) 2022/868, and Directive (EU) 2019/1024 (Digital Omnibus), COM(2025) 837 final, 19.11.2025
